explanations: terra: Rain and fruits are made رِزْقًا لَّكُمْ, a concise creation-to-provision chain opposite a plant offered without nourishment.
luna: The section's “طعام” is a single thorny food that fails to nourish; here the Israelites ask for varied earth-grown foods instead of one food, distinguishing monotony from starvation.

luna: The section labels جوع as hunger; here “الجوع” is one hardship in a test, a different frame from the section's punitive hunger that even food cannot relieve. | terra: الجُوع is a divinely announced trial alongside fear and loss; unlike the final fixed hunger of the section, this hunger is limited by “something of” and calls for patient response.
terra: Those who conceal revelation “eat into their bellies nothing but fire”; the eating-and-belly vocabulary turns apparent intake into the very opposite of nourishment.

terra: A fruit garden is struck by a fiery whirlwind precisely when its aged owner and weak offspring need it; provision turns to ash at the point of greatest dependence, a sharp indirect parallel to food that cannot answer need.

terra: The unknowing count restrained poor people أَغْنِيَاءَ; the ayah distinguishes apparent sufficiency from real hidden need, sharpening the section's concern with what food is called and what condition it actually leaves.
terra: Wealth and children لَن تُغْنِيَ عَنْهُمْ against God; possessions fail to create the needlessness that the section's غ ن ي definition associates with possessions.
terra: The same warning is repeated: wealth and children will not avail against God, fixing a boundary on material “sufficiency.”
terra: A bitterly cold wind destroys the crop of people who wronged themselves; the parable turns cultivated food into loss, another specific passage from expected nourishment to ruined vegetation.

terra: The orphan-guardian rule places غَنِيًّا opposite فَقِيرًا and allows the poor guardian to “eat” reasonably; it concretely joins economic sufficiency, need, and eating, the three senses unfolded in the section.
terra: Those who consume orphans' wealth unjustly are in fact eating fire into their bellies, another exact case of eating that fills the body only with punishment.

luna: The section's named root جوع describes hunger left unresolved; this verse permits otherwise forbidden food for someone in severe hunger, showing food preserving life where the section's sole food cannot. | terra: After listing forbidden foods, the ayah permits necessity under severe hunger; the legal boundary itself recognizes that hunger is a bodily lack food must answer.
terra: Jesus and Mary both “used to eat food”; the ordinary need to eat marks creaturely dependence and helps explain why food that does not answer hunger is such complete deprivation.
terra: Feeding ten poor people is measured by the average food one gives one's own family, supplying a concrete Quranic standard for food adequate enough to count as feeding.
terra: The disciples ask whether a table can be sent from heaven; this ayah stages the requested food-object whose purposes 5:113-114 then make explicit.

terra: The disciples want to eat from the heavenly table and have their hearts reassured; the meal is expected to answer both bodily and inward lack, exactly the two-function test applied to food in the section.
terra: Jesus asks for the table as a feast, a sign, and provision and calls God the best Provider; this is food whose abundance of functions directly reverses the uselessness of ضَرِيع.
terra: God grants the table but attaches an unparalleled punishment to disbelief afterward, marking bestowed food as both provision and a test rather than an automatic guarantee of safety.

luna: The section depicts people dependent on food that cannot feed them; this verse calls God the one who “يطعم ولا يطعم,” the provider who is not himself in need. | terra: وَهُوَ يُطْعِمُ وَلَا يُطْعَمُ distinguishes the God who feeds from creatures who need feeding, clarifying the section's opposition between need and true sufficiency.

luna: The section links the ض ر ع family to severe need; this verse's “لعلهم يتضرعون” describes people driven by adversity to humble appeal, a response of need rather than sufficiency. | terra: The section's dictionary branch defines ضراعة as displayed extreme need; يَتَضَرَّعُونَ here is the hoped-for pleading after hardship and adversity make that need felt.
terra: تَضَرَّعُوا names the humble pleading that should have followed punishment, while hard hearts prevent acknowledgment of need; it continues the ضراعة branch developed in the section.
luna: The section labels the ض ر ع family with need and poverty; here people call on God “تضرعا وخفية” while seeking rescue at sea, an explicit appeal from helpless need.
terra: A boiling drink is assigned as recompense, a direct instance of drink serving torment rather than answering bodily need.
terra: Rain produces green growth, grain, date clusters, vines, olives, and pomegranates; this ripening abundance is the plant-world reverse of dried ضَرِيع.
terra: Livestock are made for carrying loads and for food, and people are told to eat God's provision; the animal and Provider details meet the section's ewe and nourishment images.

terra: The people of the Fire ask the people of the Garden for water or some of God's provision and are told both are forbidden to rejecters; unrelieved need and true provision confront one another in one scene.

luna: The section's dictionary sense of ضراعة is intense need; this verse repeats hardship leading people to “يضرعون,” making dependence audible as supplication. | terra: Peoples are seized with hardship and adversity so that they might humble themselves; the ض ر ع form turns affliction into manifest need, the human-state sense heard beside ضَرِيع.
terra: If believers fear poverty, God promises to enrich them from His bounty; this uses the غ ن ي family for relief of material need, the successful sense denied in لَا يُغْنِي مِن جُوعٍ.
terra: The ayah pairs just recompense for believers with a boiling drink for rejecters; the drink is an anti-provision produced by the judgment scene.

terra: Earth's vegetation flourishes with rain until it is suddenly reaped as though it had not existed; the plant's passage from apparent abundance to nothing supports the section's dried, empty provision image.
terra: Seven fat cows are eaten by seven lean ones, beside green ears and dry ears; the dream gathers the section's fatness-versus-emaciation and living-versus-dried plant contrasts in one scene.
terra: The dream is repeated as سَبْعِ بَقَرَاتٍ سِمَانٍ consumed by lean cows with green and dry ears, preserving both the س م ن root and the dry-food crisis.
terra: Joseph tells them to leave the harvest in its ears except the little they eat; this gives the dream's fat and dry images their concrete meaning as conserved nourishment.
terra: Seven hard years consume almost all the stored crop, turning the eating imagery of the dream into an extended hunger and depletion scene.
terra: After the hard years comes rain and pressing of produce; the ayah completes the fat/lean, green/dry sequence with restored liquid and abundance.
terra: The promised Garden has food that endures and shade that endures; lasting food and functioning shade jointly reverse both ضَرِيع and the shade that does not avail in 77:31.

luna: The section names ghislin as another exceptional Hell-food; this verse describes a drink of pus, another degraded intake rather than sustaining provision. | terra: The person in Hell is made to drink festering water, a liquid provision that deepens suffering rather than relieving thirst.

luna: The section's food fails its purpose; this continuation says the pus is gulped with difficulty and brings death from every side, making ingestion itself affliction. | terra: He gulps but can scarcely swallow it and is approached by death without dying; the ayah spells out the drink's failure even at the act of consumption.
terra: The good tree gives its fruit continually by its Lord's permission, a productive plant defined by repeated nourishment rather than dryness and failure.
terra: The bad word is like a tree uprooted from the earth with no stability; it supplies the barren tree-side boundary to the fruitful tree in 14:25, though it is not itself presented as food.
terra: God sends water and brings forth fruits as provision, directly joining the Provider to food that genuinely answers need.
terra: God sends water from the sky and gives it to people to drink while they cannot store its source, clarifying who supplies the drink-side of bodily need.
terra: Livestock provide warmth, benefits, and food; they realize the bodily abundance suggested by the section's “large-uddered ewe” sense instead of leaving it unheard and unused.
terra: Water from heaven becomes drink and vegetation for grazing, combining true drink with living pasture against thin punitive drink and a dried thorn.
terra: The same water grows crops, olives, palms, grapes, and fruits, a many-sided plant provision opposite the single dry plant imposed in Hell.

luna: The section's secondary dictionary sense of ضريع includes a sheep with a large udder and a thin drink; this verse describes pure, palatable milk from livestock, a specific counterimage of drink and nourishment. | terra: Pure, palatable milk comes from livestock; it realizes the abundance heard in the section's secondary sense of ضَرِيع as a large-uddered ewe and counters its thin-drink sense.
terra: Dates and grapes yield both intoxicant and good provision; the ayah distinguishes products made from fruitful plants and identifies a genuinely good provision, unlike the single dried thorn.
terra: The bee's varied drink contains healing for people; a consumed liquid that benefits the body is the functional reverse of the section's thin-drink echo and Hell's injurious drinks.

luna: The section stages hunger despite an available but useless food; this town first receives abundant provision, then is made to taste “الجوع والخوف” after ingratitude. | terra: A secure town receives abundant provision, then is made to taste hunger and fear after ingratitude; it reverses 106:4 and makes hunger the felt withdrawal of real food.
terra: When the damned call for relief, they receive water like molten metal that scorches faces; the offered drink reverses the very relief requested.
terra: The garden owner is warned that its water may sink beyond recovery, identifying loss of drink as one route by which productive land ceases to provide.
terra: The garden's fruit is encompassed and its trellises collapse, completing the reversal from abundant produce to a provision that can no longer be gathered.

luna: The section's dictionary gloss makes dryness central to ضريع; this parable shows vegetation becoming “هشيما” scattered by wind, a related scene of plant growth ending unusable. | terra: Rain-mixed vegetation becomes dry fragments scattered by wind, another direct Quranic rendering of plant matter after nourishment and freshness have gone.
terra: Mary is told to shake the palm so fresh ripe dates fall to her; a fruit tree answers acute bodily vulnerability with accessible nourishment.
terra: “Eat, drink, and be comforted” joins food, drink, and inward relief in one command, the fullest positive opposite to a meal that neither fattens nor removes lack.
terra: Rain brings forth diverse pairs of plants, the living and varied plant-world opposite to one dried, foul food plant.
terra: “Eat and pasture your livestock” identifies those plants as effective nourishment for people and herds.

luna: The section's named root ج و ع appears in “ألا تجوع فيها”: the Garden is defined by absence of hunger, reversing the food that cannot satisfy. | terra: Adam is promised أَلَّا تَجُوعَ in the Garden; absence of hunger defines complete provision against the hell meal that leaves hunger untouched.

luna: After 20:118's Garden promise of no hunger, this neighbor adds no thirst there; it completes the reversal of food and drink that fail to relieve need. | terra: The Garden also removes thirst and exposure to heat, completing 20:118's picture of bodily needs answered rather than aggravated.

luna: The section's dictionary phrase طاعم حسن الحال links eating with bodily well-being; this verse says messengers were bodies that ate, marking ordinary food as part of embodied life and the condemned meal as a reversal.
terra: Boiling water is poured over the heads of the people of the Fire, beginning a bodily destruction scene that 22:20 carries inward.
terra: The boiling water melts what is in their bellies as well as their skins, reversing the belly-building work the section assigns to food.
terra: Pilgrims are told to eat from sacrificial animals and feed the miserable poor, a concrete distribution of nourishing food against the scene of need left intact.
terra: Sacrificial camels become food both for the worshippers and for the contented and asking poor, joining livestock nourishment to the duty of relieving another's need.
terra: Water descends in due measure and is lodged in the earth, while God can remove it; drinkable provision is both fitted to need and explicitly contingent.
terra: Rain-raised gardens contain abundant fruits from which people eat, directly opposing a plant that neither fattens nor removes hunger.
terra: The Sinai tree produces oil and relish for eaters; this is a plant defined by bodily benefit and palatability, the precise functional opposite of ضَرِيع.

luna: The section's dictionary sense of ضريع includes a large-udder sheep; this verse names cattle as drink, food, and many benefits, contrasting usable provision with the dry plant that does neither bodily job. | terra: Livestock give drink from their bellies, many benefits, and meat to eat; milk, food, and bodily benefit unite where ضَرِيع supplies none.
terra: Even punishment does not make them submit or يَتَضَرَّعُونَ; the refusal to display need is a significant reversal of the section's dictionary sense of ضراعة.
terra: If those marrying are poor, God will enrich them from His bounty; the promise supplies a social instance of need genuinely removed.

luna: The section's dictionary phrase طاعم حسن الحال connects eating with good condition; this verse repeats the human-messenger image of eating food and walking markets, making the section's failed nourishment a counterfeit of ordinary life.
terra: Pure water descends before the drinking scene of 25:49, the opposite in quality and effect to boiling or foul liquids offered in punishment.
terra: The water revives dead land and gives drink to livestock and many people, uniting living vegetation, herds, and effective relief of thirst.

luna: The section describes food that cannot feed and a secondary dictionary sense of ضريع as a thin drink; Abraham names God as the one who “يطعمني ويسقين,” supplying both. | terra: Abraham names God as the one who feeds and gives drink; the paired verbs identify true provision against the section's non-food and its secondary “thin drink” sense.

terra: Many creatures cannot carry their own provision, yet God provides for them and for people; the animal-provision scene resonates with the section's plant and sheep senses without depending on a shared food word.
terra: Water driven to barren land produces crops eaten by livestock and people; the ayah explicitly carries dry ground through growth to nourishment.
terra: Saba is told to eat from its Lord's provision amid two gardens and a good land; 34:16 then reverses this abundant food landscape into bitter, sparse growth.
terra: After Saba turns away, its two gardens are replaced by bitter fruit, tamarisk, and scant lote; productive vegetation becomes a meager plant provision strikingly close to the dried thorn meal.

luna: The section names غ ن ي as sufficiency and lack of need; this verse states that people are poor in need of God while God is “الغني,” marking the boundary between human hunger and divine sufficiency. | terra: People are الفُقَرَاءُ to God while God is الغَنِيُّ; this directly states the need-versus-sufficiency opposition used by the section to explain both ضراعة and يُغْنِي.
terra: Dead earth is revived and yields grain from which people eat, making plant life perform precisely the feeding function missing from ضَرِيع.
terra: Gardens of palms and grapes and flowing springs expand the grain scene into abundant food and drink.
terra: People eat the gardens' fruit though their hands did not create it, pointing from effective food back to its Provider.
terra: Rejecters answer a command to spend from God's provision by asking whether they should feed one God could feed; the ayah exposes misuse of divine provision language to leave hunger unanswered.
terra: Subdued livestock are ridden and eaten, making the herd an actual source of nourishment rather than merely the unused abundance suggested by “large-uddered ewe.”
terra: Livestock provide benefits and drinks, completing 36:72's food scene and directly activating the udder-and-drink secondary meanings developed in the section.
terra: Fruits and honor define the provision to which 37:62 compares Zaqqum when it asks which is the better hospitality.

luna: The section names the Zaqqūm tree as the source of the condemned meal; this verse frames that tree as the alternative to a better reception, making the meal itself a reversal of welcome. | terra: The question contrasts true hospitality with the tree of Zaqqum; it explicitly makes quality of provision, rather than the bare availability of something edible, the issue.
luna: The section identifies Zaqqūm as the food of the scene; this verse says the tree was made a trial for wrongdoers, explaining its role as an ordeal rather than nourishment.

luna: This neighbor locates the same Zaqqūm tree in the depths of Hell, adding the source's setting to the section's cited eating scene. | terra: Zaqqum is a tree growing in the root of Hell, a hell-grown plant counterpart to the section's dried thorn plant.

luna: This neighbor describes the Zaqqūm tree's emerging fruit as like devils' heads, supplying a concrete detail of the plant named in the section. | terra: Its fruit is made visually repellent before 37:66 describes eating it, marking the plant itself as punishment rather than provision.

luna: The section cites Zaqqūm eaten until bellies are filled; this verse makes fullness bodily but leaves open the section's distinction between filling and nourishing. | terra: The damned eat from the Zaqqum tree and fill their bellies; bodily filling without nourishment makes explicit the section's distinction between filling a body and relieving its lack.

luna: After the section's cited full bellies in 37:66, this verse adds a mixture of boiling water over the Zaqqūm, completing the meal's punitive scene. | terra: A mixture of boiling water follows the belly-filling food of 37:66, completing the food-and-drink torment.
luna: The section's cited meal belongs to a wider punishment scene; this neighbor says their return is to the blazing fire, locating the meal's outcome.
terra: Abundant fruit and drink in the Garden form the same surah's direct counter-scene to the boiling water and ghassaq of 38:57.
terra: حَمِيمٌ وَغَسَّاقٌ are presented for tasting in Hell, another pair of punitive liquids masquerading as provision.
terra: Water produces varied crops that then dry, yellow, and break apart; the ayah stages the precise loss of living plant abundance presupposed by dried ضَرِيع.
terra: They are dragged through boiling water and then burned in the Fire; the liquid belongs to punishment rather than refreshment.
terra: God makes livestock for riding and eating, another direct herd-as-provision scene opposite the dry plant that cannot nourish.
terra: Golden platters and cups circulate with everything souls desire, presenting serving vessels and desired intake where Hell offers only compulsory, harmful fare.

luna: The section's comparison to Zaqqūm is introduced here as “شجرة الزقوم,” identifying the tree behind the food of sinners. | terra: The Zaqqum tree begins another hell-food scene; 44:44 names it food, while its being a tree directly recalls the plant called ضَرِيع.

luna: The section's word طعام names the failed meal; here Zaqqūm is “طعام الأثيم,” making the food itself the sinners' punishment. | terra: طَعَامُ الْأَثِيمِ expressly calls Zaqqum “the food of the sinner,” a nourishment-word turned into a designation of punishment.

luna: The section's image of useless food becomes bodily torment here: the Zaqqūm mixture boils in the bellies. | terra: The food behaves like molten metal boiling in bellies, showing ingestion that injures the body instead of feeding it.

luna: This neighbor completes the section's Zaqqūm food scene by comparing the boiling in bellies to boiling hamim. | terra: Its boiling is likened to boiling water; this completes the bodily effect of the false food in 44:43-45 and joins punitive food to punitive drink.
terra: The secure inhabitants of the Garden call for every fruit, the same surah's direct abundance-and-safety opposite to Zaqqum as the sinner's food.

luna: The section gives ضريع a secondary dictionary sense of thin drink and a sheep with a large udder; this Garden scene offers rivers of milk and honey, a specific image of drink and abundance opposite to the sparse failed meal. | terra: This ayah sets rivers of unspoiled water, milk, wine, and honey against boiling water that cuts the intestines; it contains within one ayah the section's boundary between provision and intake that destroys the body.
terra: اللَّهُ الْغَنِيُّ وَأَنتُمُ الْفُقَرَاءُ repeats the same absolute contrast between divine sufficiency and creaturely need that the failed food cannot cure.
terra: Blessed water descends and grows gardens and harvest grain, the life-giving beginning of a provision scene opposite the dried thorn.
terra: Lofty palms with layered clusters add visibly full fruit to the provision scene.
terra: رِزْقًا لِّلْعِبَادِ names the growth as provision and joins it to reviving dead land, the reverse of plant matter emptied of nourishment.
terra: Abraham brings a عِجْلٍ سَمِينٍ, a fat calf offered in hospitality; the س م ن root supplies the abundant, nourishing opposite of food that لَا يُسْمِنُ.
terra: God wants neither provision from creatures nor that they feed Him; this is absolute needlessness beside the section's hungry bodies and deficient food.
terra: Naming God الرَّزَّاق completes 51:57: the One who needs no food is Himself the steadfast Provider.
terra: The blessed are told to eat and drink pleasantly for what they did; this supplies the good bodily state completed by the fruit and meat in 52:22.
terra: Fruit and desired meat are supplied to the blessed, showing food as wanted provision rather than compulsory torment.
terra: وَأَنَّهُ هُوَ أَغْنَىٰ وَأَقْنَىٰ attributes enrichment and sufficiency to God, the positive source of the state the hell food cannot produce.
terra: The criminals circulate between Hell and boiling water, making the drink inseparable from the fire it ordinarily ought to relieve.
terra: Chosen fruit in the reward scene stands opposite the same surah's compelled eating from Zaqqum.
terra: Desired bird meat adds nourishing choice to the paired reward meal, against bellies forcibly filled from the hell tree in 56:53.

luna: The section's quoted Zaqqūm comparison begins with “لآكلون من شجر من زقوم”; this verse identifies that tree as the food scene's source. | terra: The misguided deniers must eat from a tree of Zaqqum, a direct second occurrence of the hell-plant meal.

luna: The section's Zaqqūm comparison is made explicit by “فمالئون منها البطون”: bellies fill, while the section says its food still does not fatten or remove hunger. | terra: They fill their bellies from it, repeating the precise boundary developed in the section: fullness can occur without nourishment or relief.

luna: After the section's Zaqqūm and filled bellies, this verse adds drinking boiling water over it, extending failed food into harmful drink. | terra: After the Zaqqum they drink boiling water, completing a meal in which both food and drink intensify need and pain.

luna: The section's named root جوع is hunger left unrelieved; here condemned people drink like thirsty camels, so ingestion does not end need. | terra: They drink like desperately thirsty camels; the simile makes the drink's failure to satisfy thirst perceptible, parallel to food that fails hunger.

luna: After the section's cited Zaqqūm meal and drink, this verse calls the sequence the sinners' reception on Judgment Day, identifying the meal as their allotted provision. | terra: هَذَا نُزُلُهُمْ calls this damaging meal their “hospitality” on Judgment Day, another normal provision-word made grimly nonfunctional.
terra: “Have you considered what you sow?” opens a crop-provision interrogation whose answer distinguishes true nourishment from a crop that can be made debris.
terra: The question asks whether humans make the crop grow or God does, placing actual food production with the same Provider whom Abraham names in 26:79.

luna: The section's food is a dry plant that cannot nourish; this crop scene says God could make what is sown “حطاما,” exposing how food production can fail. | terra: God could make the crop حُطَامًا, shattered dry debris; this is a direct boundary between nourishing vegetation and plant matter like the section's dried thorn.

luna: After 56:65's crop made to crumble, this verse voices the growers' reaction; it continues the scene of food loss that makes need tangible. | terra: The cultivators would be left lamenting their loss, giving the ruined crop's human consequence rather than leaving the dry-plant image abstract.

luna: This completes the crop-loss scene with “بل نحن محرومون”; it gives an explicit deprivation parallel to the section's food that leaves hunger unmet. | terra: بَلْ نَحْنُ مَحْرُومُونَ names the result as deprivation, the state a food that does not remove hunger leaves intact.

luna: The section gives ضريع the secondary dictionary sense of a thin drink; this verse explicitly turns attention to the water people drink, connecting that branch to bodily need. | terra: The interrogation turns from sown food to the water people drink, matching the section's secondary drink sense of ضَرِيع.

luna: This continuation asks who sent down the water named in 56:68, adding the source of drink to the section's secondary dictionary sense of ضريع as a beverage. | terra: The ayah asks whether people send drinking water down or God does, identifying the source of the relief absent from hell's punitive drink.

luna: This continuation says the drinking water could have been made bitter; it marks the boundary between drink that can relieve need and the section's intake that cannot. | terra: God could make the water bitter; this explicit reversal shows that a substance can keep the appearance of drink while losing its relieving function.

luna: The section identifies ضريع as a dried plant; this verse likewise follows vegetation from growth to yellowing and “حطاما,” making its dry-plant image a transience boundary. | terra: Worldly growth pleases its cultivators, then dries, yellows, and becomes debris; the visible passage from lush plant to dry remnant illuminates how ضَرِيع names a plant in its depleted state.
terra: Neither wealth nor children will avail against God; this is another concrete case where what appears to supply worldly sufficiency fails in the judgment setting.
terra: “Who could provide for you if He withheld His provision?” makes food-sufficiency contingent on the Provider, the premise stated personally by Abraham in 26:79.
terra: The question asks who could bring flowing water if people's water sank away; it makes the availability of relieving drink depend upon the Provider.
terra: A visitation from the Lord strikes the owners' food garden while they sleep, beginning a scene in which expected produce is withheld.
terra: The garden becomes like a stripped or harvested field; productive vegetation has become empty plant-remnant, close to the section's dried thorn image.
terra: The owners resolve that no poor person will enter the garden, making deliberate denial of food to the needy part of the scene that ends in their own deprivation.
terra: On recognizing the ruined garden they say that they are deprived; the word “deprived” states the same unremoved lack reached after the crop is lost.
terra: The recipient is “in a pleasing life” before being told to eat and drink in 69:24; that good condition realizes the section's dictionary observation that a well-fed person is in a good state.
terra: كُلُوا وَاشْرَبُوا هَنِيئًا is the paired answer to 69:36: the righteous are told to eat and drink pleasantly where the condemned receive ghislin.
terra: مَا أَغْنَىٰ عَنِّي مَالِيَهْ says his wealth did not avail him; the nearby hell-food scene turns the section's غ ن ي wordplay into a double failure of wealth and food to remove need.

luna: The section's quoted ghislin passage is preceded by “ولا يحض على طعام المسكين”; this context links the punished person's deprivation to his failure to urge feeding the poor. | terra: The condemned person did not urge feeding the poor; in the same passage 69:36 gives him only ghislin, making failed human feeding and punitive non-food answer one another.

luna: The section quotes the preceding “ليس له ... حميم” before the food exception; the absence of a close companion makes the deprivation social as well as alimentary. | terra: فَلَيْسَ لَهُ ... حَمِيمٌ begins with absolute deprivation; 69:36 then adds the sole food exception, reproducing the section's ordered movement from “there is none” to “except.”

luna: The section's wording “no food except” is repeated here as “ولا طعام إلا من غسلين”; a second Hell-food sharpens the image of an exception that cannot be ordinary nourishment. | terra: The clause وَلَا طَعَامٌ إِلَّا مِنْ غِسْلِينٍ repeats the section's strict absence-plus-exception form: the only “food” is itself punishment.

luna: The section quotes this continuation of the ghislin scene: “لا يأكله إلا الخاطئون” identifies who must eat the exceptional food. | terra: This ayah says only the sinners eat that ghislin; it completes 69:36 by identifying the punitive food's fitting consumers rather than treating it as ordinary nourishment.

luna: The section's food does not satisfy; this “طعاما ذا غصة” instead lodges in the throat, presenting eating that brings neither comfort nor relief. | terra: طَعَامًا ذَا غُصَّةٍ is food that sticks in the throat, another food whose normal life-sustaining function has become torment.

luna: The section's food scene is for the punished; this confession, “ولم نك نطعم المسكين,” connects punishment to refusing to feed the needy. | terra: “We did not feed the poor” is given as a reason for entering Saqar, a second concrete link between refusal of nourishing food and the eater's later punishment.

luna: The section gives food that cannot nourish; this righteous scene has people “يطعمون الطعام” to the needy, orphan, and captive, turning food into actual care. | terra: The righteous give food they value to the poor, orphan, and captive; food here truly passes toward need rather than preserving deprivation.
luna: The section's failed meal is set against the previous verse's feeding; this neighbor states the givers seek God's face rather than repayment or thanks.
terra: Garden shade is brought close and fruit clusters are lowered within reach, pairing effective shelter with accessible food against the false shade and false meal of punishment.
terra: Their Lord gives them a pure drink, a direct positive reversal of punitive drink and of the thin-drink sense heard beside ضَرِيع.

luna: The section cites 77:31's shade that cannot protect; this preceding verse directs the deniers toward that apparent shade, setting up the failed refuge. | terra: The command to proceed to a three-branched “shade” stages the object whose failure 77:31 then states, just as 88:6 names the food before 88:7 tests its functions.

luna: The section's food “does not relieve hunger” (root غ ن ي as named there); “ولا يغني من اللهب” uses the same failure-formula for shade that cannot protect from the flame. | terra: The supposed shade is لَا ظَلِيلٍ وَلَا يُغْنِي مِنَ اللَّهَبِ: it neither shades nor avails against flame, exactly the section's image of a thing retaining its name while failing both functions, with the same يُغْنِي construction.

luna: The section cites the deniers' ineffective shade in 77:31; this verse gives the God-fearing shade and springs, a specific effective counterpart. | terra: The God-fearing are in real shade and springs, directly reversing the non-shading “shade” of 77:30-31.

luna: The section's food leaves hunger unmet; this continuation gives the God-fearing fruit they desire, the nourishing counterpart in the same surah's afterlife scene. | terra: They receive fruits they desire; the continuing contrast replaces the condemned person's false shelter and provision with wanted food.

luna: The section cites food that does not satisfy; this verse tells the God-fearing to eat and drink pleasantly, a direct reversal of the failed meal. | terra: “Eat and drink pleasantly” supplies the functional meal opposite the earlier shade that does not avail against flame.
terra: Abundant pouring water begins the growth sequence, contrasting both the dry plant and the hell drinks that cannot relieve.
terra: The water brings forth grain and plants, productive vegetation rather than dried thorn.
terra: Dense gardens complete the rain-to-food scene with abundance.

luna: This precedes the section's cited exception in 78:25: the condemned “لا يذوقون فيها بردا ولا شرابا,” a no-relief pattern parallel to no food that eases hunger. | terra: The damned taste neither coolness nor drink; the double negation establishes deprivation before 78:25 supplies its punitive exception.

luna: The section says no food except ضريع; here the corresponding thirst scene has no drink except “حميمًا وغساقًا,” a painful exception rather than relief. | terra: إِلَّا حَمِيمًا وَغَسَّاقًا answers the absence of drink with boiling water and foul discharge, the same “nothing except a harmful substitute” structure as ضَرِيع.
terra: Gardens and grapes begin the reward scene paired with 78:24-25's absence of coolness and punitive drink.
terra: A brimming cup supplies the drink-side reversal of the boiling water and ghassaq in 78:25.
terra: The earth's water and pasture are brought forth together, pairing drink with food for grazing animals.
terra: مَتَاعًا لَّكُمْ وَلِأَنْعَامِكُمْ names water and pasture as provision for people and livestock, directly answering the section's plant, hunger, and ewe imagery.

luna: The section's word طعام is reconsidered in “فلينظر الإنسان إلى طعامه”; the following verses show food as a provision made to sustain life, unlike ضريع. | terra: The command to look at one's food opens a detailed account of how real nourishment is made, a deliberate counter-image to food that fails as food.

luna: The section's dry plant cannot nourish; this verse begins the provision sequence after 80:24 by describing water poured down for food to grow. | terra: Water is poured abundantly as the first cause in the food sequence, joining nourishment and drink.

luna: The section names a dried plant; this neighbor describes earth split open in the productive chain that leads to the food listed next. | terra: The earth is split open so food can emerge, advancing the production scene toward edible plants.

luna: The section's “no food except” is contrasted with “حبّا,” grain among the foods God brings forth in the sequence begun at 80:24. | terra: Grain is grown from it, the staple nourishment opposite a dried thorn.

luna: This continuation names grapes and green fodder, concrete produce in contrast to the section's dry thorn that does not nourish. | terra: Grapes and fresh herbage extend the food scene to human produce and grazing vegetation.
luna: This continuation names olives and palms among the provisions that answer the section's failed food. | terra: Olives and palms add oil-bearing and fruit-bearing trees to the abundance.

luna: This continuation adds densely planted gardens to the food sequence, reversing the single useless thorn meal. | terra: Dense gardens supply the cultivated setting for the foods enumerated around this ayah.

luna: The section names a plant dry as thorn; this continuation names fruit and pasture, food-bearing growth rather than a meal that fails. | terra: Fruit and pasture place human food beside livestock feed, especially pertinent to the section's large-uddered-ewe echo.

luna: The section denies food's two functions; this sequence ends by calling its produce “متاعا لكم ولأنعامكم,” provision for people and livestock. | terra: The whole sequence is provision for people and their livestock, explicitly naming the beneficiaries of the effective food system.

luna: The section's dictionary description calls ضريع dried شبرق; this verse stages pasture being brought forth, the living growth before a plant dries. | terra: God brings forth pasture, the living plant stage before 87:5 turns it into dark stubble; that transformation closely matches the plant that is called ضَرِيع when dried.

luna: The section develops the dry-plant sense of ضريع; “فجعله غثاء أحوى” shows pasture becoming dark stubble, while leaving open the section's irony that this dried plant is imposed as food. | terra: The pasture becomes غُثَاءً أَحْوَىٰ, dried dark debris; it is the closest non-hell plant parallel to the section's emphasis that shibriq acquires its grim name after drying.

luna: The section's word طعام occurs in the Qur'anic rebuke “ولا تحاضون على طعام المسكين”; it makes the opposite of nourishing food a social refusal to encourage feeding. | terra: Failure to urge feeding the poor names a social withholding of food; it is the worldly human counterpart to the section's final scene of need left unrelieved.

luna: The section's word طعام fails precisely at hunger; “إطعام في يوم ذي مسغبة” is the human act of giving food when hunger is acute. | terra: إِطْعَامٌ فِي يَوْمٍ ذِي مَسْغَبَةٍ makes feeding on a day of severe hunger the saving ascent, the ethical reverse of leaving someone with food that cannot remove hunger.
luna: The section's image of unrelieved hunger is answered by 90:14's feeding on a day of hunger; this neighbor specifies the recipient as a related orphan.
luna: Continuing 90:14's food given on a hungry day, this verse names a poor person in dust, showing who receives real relief.

luna: The section names root غ ن ي and its sense of sufficiency; this verse portrays one who withholds and considers himself free of need, a false sufficiency set against the image's real, unrelieved hunger. | terra: The miser “deems himself self-sufficient” with اسْتَغْنَىٰ; 92:11 will expose that imagined sufficiency when his wealth cannot avail him.
terra: وَمَا يُغْنِي عَنْهُ مَالُهُ says wealth does not avail when he falls, joining the section's functional يُغْنِي sense to the dictionary sense of wealth and showing both fail together.

luna: The section identifies غ ن ي with sufficiency and lack of need; “فأغنى” names God making the needy Prophet free of want, opposite to food that “لا يغني” from hunger. | terra: God found the addressee عَائِلًا and made him sufficient, using أَغْنَى for an actual passage from need to sufficiency rather than the failure expressed by لَا يُغْنِي.
terra: أَن رَّآهُ اسْتَغْنَىٰ identifies perceived self-sufficiency as the ground of human transgression, a moral boundary around the section's dictionary sense of being without need.

luna: The section labels جوع as the hunger that food fails to remove; this verse says God “أطعمهم من جوع,” the direct opposite, and pairs relief from hunger with safety from fear. | terra: أَطْعَمَهُم مِّن جُوعٍ states the exact successful opposite: God feeds them out of hunger, so true food performs the removal that ضَرِيع cannot.

luna: The section's food cannot end hunger; this rebuke of the denier names failure to urge “طعام المسكين,” a human refusal to answer hunger. | terra: The one who denies judgment does not urge feeding the poor, tying disbelief to allowing another's food-need to remain exactly what it was.
terra: مَا أَغْنَىٰ عَنْهُ مَالُهُ repeats the pointed paradox that wealth itself does not make its owner free of ultimate need.
